analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax collected by the states.
analysis.headline: The bill to replace income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax was introduced in July 2003, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have repealed the entire federal tax system on income — individual and corporate income taxes, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes — and shut down the IRS, replacing all of it with a 23% tax on what people buy, collected mostly by state governments. Every family would get a monthly government check rebating the tax owed on purchases up to the poverty line. Money spent by businesses, used for investment, or exported would go untaxed, and stocks, bonds, and other securities would never be taxed at all.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gains would go to households living on accumulated wealth: capital gains, dividends, interest, inheritances, and corporate profits would face no federal tax, because only consumption is taxed and wealthy families spend a small share of their assets. Workers would stop seeing payroll taxes and withholding, and the poorest households would be shielded by the monthly poverty-level rebate. States that collect the tax would keep a fee, and retailers would be paid to remit it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy households, investors, and corporate shareholders

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal individual and corporate income taxes, all Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift taxes, effective January 2005.
Abolishes the IRS and replaces it with a Sales Tax Bureau and an Excise Tax Bureau, ending annual income tax filings for individuals.

Sends every registered family a monthly rebate — the "family consumption allowance" — equal to the tax rate times the federal poverty level for the family's size, so no family pays the tax on poverty-level spending.
Exempts purchases made for business, investment, or export, and excludes stocks, bonds, and other intangible property from the tax entirely.

Lets states that already run sales taxes collect the federal tax and keep a one-quarter of one percent administration fee, and pays sellers the greater of $200 a month or 0.25% of tax remitted for collecting it.

analysis.who_pays: Households that spend nearly everything they earn — most working and middle-class families — would pay the 23% tax on virtually every dollar, stacked on top of state sales taxes, including on rent, newly built homes, and services. Meanwhile the tax on wealth itself disappears: nothing would ever be levied on investment gains, large inheritances, or accumulated savings. Social Security and Medicare would be funded from the sales tax through general revenue, making benefits dependent on a single consumption-tax stream.
analysis.who_pays_short: Working families who spend most of their income

drawbacks.text: Every purchase — including rent, newly built homes, medical care, and services — would carry a 23% federal tax on top of state sales taxes; because lower- and middle-income households spend nearly all their income, they would pay the tax on almost everything, while savings and investment returns, concentrated among the wealthy, would go untaxed.

Repealing the estate tax and exempting securities and other intangibles means large accumulated fortunes would never face federal tax at any point — not when earned, not when invested, not when passed to heirs.

To keep receiving the monthly rebate, each family must register annually with the tax authority, listing the Social Security number of every member and certifying that all are lawful residents; a missed registration cuts off the payments.
Social Security and Medicare funding would shift from dedicated payroll taxes to general revenue raised by the sales tax, leaving benefits tied to consumer spending levels and annual appropriations.

The bill set the rate by formula (14.91% for general revenue plus the Social Security and Medicare rates in 2005's 23% combined rate) while repealing the taxes that fund the entire government; if the rate raised less than the taxes it replaced, the result would be borrowing, benefit cuts, or rate increases later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification is real — no tax filings, no withholding, no estate tax — and the poverty-level rebate does protect the poorest households. But the arithmetic favors those who live on accumulated wealth: under this design only spending is ever taxed, so the more of your money you can afford not to spend, the less tax you pay. A family living paycheck to paycheck sees nearly every dollar taxed at 23%, while a household living off untaxed dividends and an untaxed inheritance pays tax only on the fraction it spends. Honest supporters would also have to acknowledge that shifting the entire federal funding base to one rate is a gamble — if it fell short, the choices would be deficits or cutting Social Security and Medicare.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never came back out — no hearing, no markup, no floor debate, no vote — before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Saxby Chambliss (R-GA) introduced the bill on July 30, 2003; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill; no other member of the Senate acted on it.

The Finance Committee took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the bill's history — and the bill received no further action of any kind before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
The bill's substance — repealing income, payroll, and estate taxes and replacing them with a 23% consumption tax — was never debated or voted on in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Middle- and working-income households came out ahead: they kept the existing income tax, which takes a smaller share of a paycheck-to-paycheck family's income than a 23% tax on every purchase would. The wealthiest households lost the chance to see investment returns, corporate profits, and inheritances permanently exempted from federal tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Middle-income families who kept the income tax

for.name: Sen. Saxby Chambliss
for.role: U.S. Senator from Georgia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the Senate floor; it was referred to the Finance Committee and never moved again.

for.name: One Democratic senator
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators joined.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican; controls whether tax bills get a hearing or vote
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee from July 2003 until the Congress ended with no action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no party split exists in the record: a Republican sponsored the bill, a single Democratic senator cosponsored it, and the Senate — where Republicans held the majority and the Finance Committee chair — never brought it up.

industries.note: Capital gains, dividends, interest, and inheritances would never be taxed, and only consumption would be — which wealthy families can keep low relative to their wealth. The revenue gap is filled by taxing everything every other household buys.
The corporate income tax is part of the repealed income tax subtitle, so corporate profits would face no federal tax. The tax burden shifts to consumers at the register.

industries.industry: Financial services and the investment industry
industries.note: Stocks, bonds, and other securities are defined as intangibles excluded from tax, and investment purchases are exempt, so capital would flow untaxed; only fees for financial intermediation services would be taxed.
States with sales taxes would collect the federal tax and keep a 0.25% administration fee, expanding their role in federal tax collection.
New homes and rents would carry the 23% federal tax while existing homes would not, raising the cost of the largest purchase most families ever make.

Stores would take on collection and remittance duties and post bonds, but would be compensated with a credit of the greater of $200 a month or 0.25% of tax remitted, and their own business purchases would be tax-free.
